questions.stem: A chemical is found in a river at concentrations above natural background levels. No adverse ecological effects are observed. The chemical is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Contamination means the compound is present at concentrations above background level; Pollution means the compound causes adverse effect on human or ecological systems.

questions.stem: According to the Brundtland Report, sustainable development requires:

options.text: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations needs
Unlimited resource extraction for economic growth
Balancing environmental protection with quality-of-life improvement

questions.explanation: Development should satisfy current needs while preserving the ability of future generations to satisfy theirs, that means-Present generation must benefit (quality of life); Future generations must not suffer; and Environment must be protected Option B violates sustainability because unlimited extraction leads to resource depletion.

questions.stem: A researcher obtains the following R� values while fitting population data: Model A: 0.32 Model B: 0.71 Model C: 0.96 Which model best describes the observed data?
questions.explanation: R� measures goodness of fit. R2 >0.9, it is a reasonably good fit and >0.95 is a very good fit. Values of R2 <0.5 show that there is no correlation between the two independent variables.

questions.stem: If a class has a capacity for 100 students now, and the capacity for students is to be increased by 10% every year, what will the student intake capacity be at the end of 30 years?
questions.explanation: As P0 = 100, n = number of years = 30 and r = 10% or 0.1 P=P0*exp (n*r) = 100*exp (30*0.1) = 2008

questions.stem: A country successfully reduces its population growth rate but doubles its per-capita resource consumption. What is the most likely outcome?
questions.explanation: Environmental impact depends on: Population � Consumption � Technology So, if population growth decreases, a large increase in consumption can offset the gains. This is why some low-population countries still have very high environmental footprints.

questions.stem: Which of the following are correctly classified as renewable resources?
questions.explanation: renewable resource can naturally restore within a reasonable time scale. Air is continuously renewed through atmospheric processes. Water is renewed through the hydrologic cycle.

questions.stem: Organic matter discharged into a river is decomposed/degraded naturally. This ability or self-purification capacity of a river is an example of:
questions.explanation: The river is performing an ecological function. The water itself is a resource. Its ability to assimilate and degrade wastes is a service provided by nature.

questions.stem: A city imports food, fuel, and manufactured products while exporting large amounts of waste. This city most closely resembles:
questions.explanation: Petropolis is characterized by: Dependence on fossil fuels, Heavy transportation requirements, Import of goods and services Export of wastes

questions.stem: Two buildings use identical construction materials. Building X minimizes energy use only during operation. Building Y minimizes energy and resource use throughout manufacturing, operation, maintenance, and disposal. Which is more consistent with sustainable design?
questions.explanation: Green design mostly focuses on reducing current environmental impacts. Sustainable design considers the entire lifecycle: Manufacturing, Transportation, Operation, Maintenance, Disposal. Therefore, Building Y represents sustainable design.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental weakness of a linear economy?

options.text: Resources move in a one-way flow from extraction to disposal.

questions.explanation: Linear Economy: Take Make Dispose Resources are extracted, converted into products, and discarded. This model ignores material recovery.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes would move a city from a Petropolis toward an Ecopolis?
questions.explanation: An Ecopolis: Reduce external dependence, minimize waste, Close material loops, use renewable resources so, Local production, Recycling and Renewable energy support the transition. Increasing fossil-fuel imports does the opposite.

questions.stem: If a country doubles its electricity generation using coal while maintaining the same population. What is the most likely environmental consequence?
questions.explanation: Coal: Non-renewable and Carbon intensive Doubling coal-based generation implies: More coal extraction More combustion More CO emissions More air pollution Greater environmental burden. Thus, environmental impacts increase even without population growth.

questions.stem: The Capital Stock Model suggests that sustainable development is achieved when:

options.text: Society lives on interest rather than capital

questions.explanation: The lecture compares sustainability to living on the interest generated by capital rather than consuming the capital itself. Consuming the capital stock threatens long- term prosperity.

questions.stem: Population = 200 million, Per capita electricity use = 1500 kWh/person-year, CO2 Emission factor = 0.9 kg/kWh, Calculate Total annual CO emissions?
Which of the following are pillars of sustainable development?
questions.explanation: The three pillars correspond to social, environmental, and economic/financial dimensions.

questions.stem: Which represent ecological deficit?
questions.explanation: Deficit occurs when: EF>BC

questions.stem: Earth Overshoot Day represents:

options.text: The day humanity's resource demand exceeds Earth's annual regeneration capacity
The first day of the year
The day carbon emissions become zero

questions.explanation: Earth Overshoot Day is the date when humanity has consumed all ecological resources that Earth can regenerate during that year. After this day, humanity is operating on an ecological deficit.

questions.stem: A building consumes 60,000 kWh/year, Area = 1,500 m�, Calculate EPI.
questions.explanation: EPI = [Annual Energy Consumption/Floor Area] = [60000/1500] = 40 kWh/m2-year

questions.stem: Factors affecting EPI include:
questions.explanation: Number of Occupants: More occupants generally increase lighting demand, cooling load, appliance usage. Climate and Seasonal Variations: Hot climates increase air-conditioning demand, energy consumption. Cold climates increase heating demand.

questions.stem: Which paper products generate more than 8,000 kg GHG emissions?
questions.explanation: Toilet paper = 11,897 A4 = 8,999 Paperboard = 1,495 [It is made from 100% recycled fibre, using recycled fibres eliminates many energy-intensive steps associated with producing virgin pulp. It does not require virgin wood, so no fresh trees are harvested, emissions from logging, transportation, and initial wood processing are avoided.] Newsprint = 9,681

questions.stem: According to the Planetary Boundaries Framework, several Earth-system processes have already exceeded their safe operating limits. Which of the following boundaries is considered to have been crossed?
questions.explanation: No official answer key in source. Land-system change is among boundaries assessed as crossed; ocean acidification, ozone, and freshwater were generally within safer ranges at the time of the framework updates taught in the course.

questions.stem: The Brundtland Commission was established primarily to address growing concerns about

options.text: Widening disparities between economic growth and environmental protection
Global financial instability and trade imbalances

questions.explanation: No official answer key. The Brundtland Commission was convened to address the growing gap between economic growth and environmental protection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a negative international spillover effect in the context of sustainable development?

options.text: Relocation of pollution-intensive industries from developed to developing countries
Transfer of clean-energy technologies to developing nations
Adoption of renewable energy technologies leading to reduced transboundary air pollution
International cooperation for the conservation of biodiversity

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Relocating pollution-intensive industries transfers environmental burdens across borders (negative spillover).

questions.stem: Which of the following Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is most directly focused on promoting peace, justice, strong institutions, accountability, and transparent governance?
questions.explanation: No official answer key. SDG 16 focuses on peace, justice, and strong institutions.

questions.stem: The inclusion of "Partnership" as one of the five "P's" of the SDGs underscores the importance of

options.text: international cooperation and multi-stakeholder collaboration for sustainable development
mobilizing financial resources exclusively for developed countries
promoting investment primarily in developed economies
privatizing environmental governance and public services

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Partnership among the 5 Ps emphasizes multi-stakeholder and international collaboration.

questions.stem: What is the primary significance of the SDG Index as a tool for assessing sustainable development performance?

options.text: It focuses exclusively on environmental indicators
It ranks countries based on geopolitical influence
It replaces national statistical systems for development monitoring
It offers a composite measure of progress toward achieving the SDGs.

questions.explanation: No official answer key. The SDG Index is a composite score of country progress toward the SDGs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best reflects the primary objective of Smart City initiatives?

options.text: To achieve full automation of urban services through artificial intelligence.
To minimize government involvement by promoting privately managed urban systems.
To enhance urban sustainability, efficiency, and quality of life through the integration of digital technologies and data-driven governance
To replace conventional infrastructure with futuristic urban designs and architecture.

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Smart City initiatives aim to improve sustainability, efficiency, and quality of life via digital/data-driven governance.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about extensive green roofs is correct?

options.text: They use deep layers of soil to grow large plants.
They are significantly heavier than intensive green roofs.
They use a thin layer of soil and feature easy-to-maintain vegetation.

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Extensive green roofs use a thin soil layer and low-maintenance vegetation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a significant environmental impact of the urban heat island effect?

options.text: Reduced temperature differences between urban and rural areas
Increased energy consumption for cooling in cities.
Enhanced groundwater recharge through increased infiltration.
Reduced generation of anthropogenic heat from human activities.

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Urban heat islands raise cooling energy demand in cities.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics most clearly distinguishes sustainable urbanization from conventional patterns of urban growth?

options.text: Dependence on private automobiles for mobility
Integration of environmental resilience, social inclusivity, and resource efficiency
Strict separation of residential and commercial land uses

questions.explanation: No official answer key. Sustainable urbanization integrates environmental resilience, social inclusivity, and resource efficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a secondary air pollutant, formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions involving primary pollutants?
questions.explanation: Ground-level ozone (O3) is a secondary air pollutant because it is formed in the atmosphere through reactions between nitrogen oxides (NO) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. The other options are primary pollutants emitted directly from sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following atmospheric conditions is most conducive to the formation of a radiation inversion?

options.text: Cloudy conditions that limit nighttime heat loss
Intense daytime heating of the Earth's surface
Rainfall associated with monsoon weather systems
Clear, calm nights that promote rapid surface cooling.

questions.explanation: Radiation inversions commonly occur on clear, calm nights when the ground loses heat rapidly through radiation. This cools the air near the surface more than the air above, creating a temperature inversion in which temperature increases with height.

questions.stem: Which fraction of particulate matter can penetrate deepest into the human body?
questions.explanation: Ultrafine particles (PM0.1) can translocate to multiple organs and cause severe health impacts.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) enables it to be the dominant component of transboundary haze?

options.text: They are largely insoluble in water.
They can remain suspended in the atmosphere for extended periods and be transported over long distances.
They have a short atmospheric residence time.
They are transported only under conditions of strong winds.

questions.explanation: Fine particles (PM2.5) have very low settling velocities, allowing them to remain airborne for days to weeks. As a result, they can be carried over hundreds or even thousands of kilometers by atmospheric circulation, making them a major contributor to transboundary haze.

questions.stem: In a dry atmosphere, under which condition is the atmosphere considered unstable?

options.text: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is greater than the environmental lapse rate.
The dry adiabatic lapse rate is equal to the environmental lapse rate.
The dry adiabatic lapse rate is less than the environmental lapse rate.
The moist adiabatic lapse rate is equal to the environmental lapse rate.

questions.explanation: An atmosphere is unstable when the environmental lapse rate (ELR) exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR). In this case, a rising air parcel remains warmer and less dense than its surroundings, causing it to continue rising. Therefore, atmospheric instability occurs when the DALR is less than the ELR.

questions.stem: Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) technology is an air pollution control technology primarily used to reduce emissions of ______, converting them into harmless ______ and ______.
questions.explanation: Selective catalytic reduction (SCR) is an advanced technology used to control nitrogen oxide (NO) emissions from diesel engines. In this process, a diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), typically a urea-based solution, is injected into the exhaust stream upstream of a catalyst. The heat of the exhaust converts the DEF into ammonia (NH3), which then reacts with nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) on the surface of the catalyst.

questions.stem: A region is exposed to severe acid deposition over an extended period. Which of the following environmental impacts is most likely to occur first?

options.text: Depletion of soil buffering capacity due to the loss of Ca2 and Mg2 ion.
Enhanced carbon sequestration in terrestrial ecosystems.

questions.explanation: Acid deposition leaches essential base cations such as calcium (Ca2) and magnesium (Mg2) from soils, reducing their ability to neutralize acidity. This loss of buffering capacity is typically one of the earliest environmental effects and can eventually lead to soil degradation, forest decline, and aquatic ecosystem damage.

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds is not considered an ozone-depleting substance (ODS)?
questions.explanation: Ozone depletion is primarily caused by compounds containing chlorine or bromine, which release reactive halogen radicals in the stratosphere. Methyl fluoride (CH3F) contains fluorine but no chlorine or bromine and has negligible ozone-depleting potential. In contrast, methyl chloride, methyl bromide, and methyl chloroform are recognized ozone-depleting substances.

questions.stem: A dry air parcel with an initial temperature of 30�C rises 1 km in the atmosphere. Assuming a dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR) of 9.8�C km�1 and an environmental temperature of 22�C at 1 km altitude, what will most likely happen to the parcel?

options.text: It will sink back toward the surface.
It will form a temperature inversion.

questions.explanation: The parcel cools at the DALR as it rises: Tparcel = 30-9.8 = 20.2�C At 1 km, the surrounding air temperature is 22�C, which is warmer than the parcel (20.2�C). Since the parcel is cooler and therefore denser than its surroundings, it experiences negative buoyancy and tends to sink back toward the surface. Thus, the atmosphere is stable under these conditions.

questions.stem: The sub-index values of NO, SO2, and PM10 are 60, 90, and 40, respectively. According to the National Air Quality Index (NAQI) released by the Government of India in the year 2015, the overall NAQI is
questions.explanation: According to NAQI, overall AQI equals the highest pollutant sub-index. With NO=60, SO2=90, PM10=40, NAQI=90. (Source answer key lists 'a. 90'; option labels in the text appear misaligned.)

questions.stem: Which of the following factors directly influence the atmospheric dispersion of pollutants?
questions.explanation: Atmospheric dispersion is affected by several meteorological and source-related factors. Wind speed controls the rate of pollutant transport and dilution, atmospheric stability determines the extent of vertical mixing, and emission height influences the distance pollutants travel before reaching ground level.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about ozone-depleting substances (ODSs) are correct?

options.text: ODSs are highly reactive in the troposphere.
ODSs contribute to the destruction of stratospheric ozone.

questions.explanation: CFCs and halons are well-known ODSs. After reaching the stratosphere, they release chlorine and bromine radicals that catalytically destroy ozone. Most ODSs are actually chemically stable in the troposphere, which allows them to persist long enough to reach the stratosphere.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the primary precursors involved in the formation of photochemical smog?
questions.explanation: Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides (NO) and volatile organic compounds react in the presence of sunlight. Aldehydes and PAN are secondary pollutants produced during these photochemical reactions.

questions.stem: Which of the following health effects may result from prolonged exposure to indoor air pollution?
questions.explanation: From assignment solution.

questions.stem: A pollutant is emitted at the same rate from two stacks: � Stack A: 80 m height � Stack B: 250 m height An atmospheric temperature inversion extends from the ground surface up to 200 m. Which of the following statements are most likely correct?

options.text: Pollutants from Stack A are more likely to be trapped below the inversion.
Pollutants from Stack B may disperse more effectively.
Pollutants from Stack B are more likely to be trapped below the inversion.
Pollutants from Stack A may disperse more effectively.

questions.explanation: The inversion layer extends from the surface to 200 m, so pollutants released below 200 m tend to remain trapped near the ground. � Stack A = 80 m: It releases pollutants within/below the inversion layer, so pollutants are more likely to be trapped. Hence, a is correct.

questions.stem: Climate is typically defined based on atmospheric observations averaged over what minimum time period?
questions.explanation: According to the World Meteorological Organization, climate is commonly described using averages and variability of weather-related parameters over a period of at least 30 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods is commonly used to reconstruct past atmospheric temperatures and climate conditions?

options.text: By relying solely on historical records and written documents
By analyzing tiny air bubbles preserved within ice cores
By using satellite observations collected since the 1800s

questions.explanation: Ice cores extracted from glaciers and ice sheets contain tiny air bubbles that were trapped when the ice formed. These bubbles preserve information about past atmospheric composition (e.g., CO2 and CH4 concentrations), allowing scientists to reconstruct past climate conditions and estimate historical temperatures over thousands of years.

questions.stem: If global photosynthetic activity increased significantly while fossil fuel emissions remained unchanged, how would the atmospheric CO2 record represented by the Keeling Curve most likely respond?

options.text: A reduced rate of increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration
A steeper increase in atmospheric CO2 concentration
Complete disappearance of seasonal CO2 fluctuations
No measurable change in atmospheric CO2 concentration

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the atmosphere and stores it in plant biomass. If global photosynthetic activity increased substantially, more CO2 would be absorbed from the atmosphere, partially offsetting fossil fuel emissions. As a result, the Keeling Curve would still show rising atmospheric CO2 concentrations, but the rate of increase would be slower than before.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the influence of anthropogenic aerosols on Earth's climate?

options.text: They contribute only to climate warming.
They contribute only to climate cooling.
They have no significant effect on climate.
They can exert both warming and cooling effects on climate.

questions.explanation: Different aerosols affect climate in different ways. Sulfate aerosols generally cool the climate by reflecting incoming solar radiation, whereas black carbon (soot) absorbs sunlight and contributes to warming. Aerosols can also modify cloud properties, leading to additional cooling or warming effects.

questions.stem: One carbon credit represents the offset of 1 tonne of CO2 equivalent (CO2e). A coal-fired power plant emits 2.5 kg of CO2 per kWh of electricity generated and operates continuously at a capacity of 500 MW throughout the year (365 days). How many carbon credits would be required annually to offset 50% of the plant's CO2 emissions? How many would be required to offset 100% of its emissions?
questions.explanation: Annual electricity generation = 500 MW � 365 days � 24 h/day = 4,380,000 MWh = 4.38 � 109 kWh Annual CO2 emissions = 2.5 kg/kWh � 4.38 � 109 kWh = 1.095 � 1010 kg = 1.095 � 107 tons Since 1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e: � Credits for 100% offset = 10,950,000 � Credits for 50% offset = 10,950,000 / 2 = 5,475,000

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reliable indicator of climate change that is directly linked to rising ocean temperatures?

options.text: Rise in global average sea levels
Increased volcanic activity on the ocean floor

questions.explanation: Rising ocean temperatures contribute directly to sea level rise through two primary mechanisms: thermal expansion � as seawater warms, it expands, increasing sea volume, and melting of glaciers and ice sheets � warmer oceans accelerate the melting of ice shelves and glaciers that feed into the sea. As a result, the rise in global average sea levels is a direct and measurable indicator of climate change, closely linked to increasing ocean temperatures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not generally classified as a geoengineering strategy for mitigating climate change?
questions.explanation: Geoengineering typically refers to large-scale deliberate interventions in the Earth's climate system, such as ocean fertilization, stratospheric aerosol injection, and marine cloud brightening. These are examples of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) or solar radiation management (SRM) approaches. In contrast, deep-ocean storage of CO2 is generally considered a carbon capture and storage (CCS) technique rather than a geoengineering strategy.

questions.stem: Permafrost thaw and subsidence will directly lead to

options.text: addition of more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere

questions.explanation: In the Arctic, large amounts of organic carbon are stored in permafrost. The carbon in the permafrost has built up over thousands of years, as dead plants have been buried and accumulated within layers of frozen soil, where the cold prevents the organic material from decomposing. As the Arctic warms and soils thaw, the organic matter in these soils will decompose rapidly and return to the atmosphere as CO2 or CH4, both important greenhouse gases that further warm the Arctic.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): The Kyoto Protocol imposed legally binding greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reduction targets on developing countries. Reason (R): Under the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR), developing countries were exempted from binding emission reduction targets during the first commitment period of the Kyoto Protocol.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol established binding emission reduction targets for developed (Annex I) countries, not developing countries. The exemption of developing countries was based on the CBDR principle, which recognizes differing historical responsibilities and capacities among nations.

questions.stem: Match the concepts in List I with their correct descriptions in List II. List I (Concepts) List II (Descriptions)

options.text: Oxyfuel combustion 1. Fuel is burned in nearly pure oxygen, producing

Post-combustion capture a flue gas consisting mainly of CO2 and H2O. 2. A gas separation process that uses liquid solvents to selectively remove CO2. 3. Fuel is converted into synthesis gas (syngas), and CO2 is separated before hydrogen is
Absorption combusted. 4. CO2 is removed from flue gas after the fuel has been combusted.

questions.stem: Which of the following are major greenhouse gases that occur naturally in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and water vapor (H2O) are naturally occurring greenhouse gases that help regulate Earth's temperature. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are synthetic compounds produced by human activities and do not occur naturally in the atmosphere, although they are potent greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the role of the ocean in Earth's climate system are correct?

options.text: The ocean has no significant influence on atmospheric CO2 concentrations.
The ocean absorbs approximately one-quarter of anthropogenic CO2 emissions.
Thermal expansion of seawater contributes to global sea-level rise.
The ocean's large heat capacity and thermal inertia can delay surface warming over long timescales.

questions.explanation: The ocean is a major regulator of Earth's climate. It absorbs roughly 25% of human-generated CO2 emissions, helping to moderate atmospheric CO2 levels. As ocean water warms, it expands, contributing to sea-level rise.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors can influence Earth's energy budget?

options.text: The extent of sea ice and seasonal snow cover
The magnitude of ocean heat uptake

questions.explanation: All four factors affect Earth's energy balance. Land-use changes alter surface albedo and energy fluxes. Anthropogenic aerosols influence the absorption and reflection of solar radiation and can modify cloud properties.

questions.stem: Which of the following are examples of cascading climate impacts?

options.text: Melting ice reduces Earth's albedo, leading to additional warming and further ice loss.
Sea-level rise increases the risk of storm-surge flooding, causing infrastructure damage and economic losses.
Rising temperatures reduce crop yields, leading to higher food prices and adverse health outcomes.
An isolated impact that remains confined to a single sector without triggering secondary effects.

questions.explanation: Cascading climate impacts occur when an initial climate-related change triggers a chain of interconnected consequences across environmental, social, or economic systems. Options a, b, and c illustrate such cascading effects. Option d is not a cascading impact because it involves no secondary or downstream consequences.

questions.stem: Which of the following are primary functions of the IPCC?

options.text: Reviewing and synthesizing the latest climate science data from peer-reviewed literature
Conducting original climate research and experiments
Assessing the socioeconomic impacts of climate change
Producing reports that inform global policy on climate change adaptation and mitigation

questions.explanation: The IPCC primarily reviews existing scientific literature (a), assesses climate change impacts, including socioeconomic aspects (c), and produces reports to guide global climate policy (d). It does not conduct original research or experiments (b).

questions.stem: A country decides to rapidly phase out fossil fuels without investing adequately in alternative energy infrastructure. Which dimension of the Global Energy Trilemma is most likely to be adversely affected in the short term? I. Energy security II. Energy equity III. Environmental sustainability
questions.explanation: The most immediate and direct consequence is a reduction in the reliability and resilience of energy supply, which affects energy security. Effects on energy equity are possible but not certain from the information provided, while environmental sustainability would generally improve.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a Trombe wall are correct? I. It is a passive solar heating system. II. It stores solar energy in a high thermal-mass wall. III. It requires photovoltaic panels to generate electricity. IV. It can help reduce space-heating demand in buildings.
questions.explanation: A Trombe wall is a passive solar design feature consisting of a sun-facing glazed wall with high thermal mass that absorbs, stores, and gradually releases heat to the building interior. It does not require photovoltaic panels and is intended for thermal energy management rather than electricity generation.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): Bifacial photovoltaic (PV) modules can generate more electricity than monofacial PV modules under suitable operating conditions. Reason (R): Bifacial PV modules are capable of capturing solar radiation from both their front and rear surfaces.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The assertion is true because bifacial PV modules can produce more electricity than conventional monofacial modules when installed under favorable conditions. The reason is also true, as bifacial modules are designed to capture solar radiation on both sides of the panel. In addition to direct sunlight incident on the front surface, the rear surface can utilize reflected and diffuse radiation from the ground and surrounding surfaces (albedo radiation).

questions.stem: Which of the following concentrating solar power (CSP) technologies is the most commercially mature and accounts for the largest share of installed CSP capacity worldwide?
questions.explanation: Parabolic trough systems are the most established CSP technology, with extensive commercial deployment and operational experience across many large-scale solar thermal power plants worldwide.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of thermal energy storage in a concentrating solar power (CSP) plant?

options.text: To store excess thermal energy for electricity generation during periods of low or no solar radiation
To increase the concentration ratio of solar collectors
To convert solar energy directly into electricity without a turbine
To eliminate heat losses from the solar receiver

questions.explanation: Thermal energy storage systems, commonly based on molten salts, store heat collected during sunny periods and release it later to generate electricity when sunlight is unavailable, thereby improving the dispatchability of CSP plants.

questions.stem: According to Betz's law, a wind turbine cannot extract all of the kinetic energy from the wind because

options.text: the air must retain some kinetic energy after passing through the rotor.
the wind speed must remain unchanged across the rotor plane.
the air accelerates as it passes through the rotor, reducing energy extraction.
the kinetic energy of the wind is independent of its velocity.

questions.explanation: A wind turbine generates power by extracting a portion of the wind's kinetic energy and reducing its velocity. However, the air must retain some kinetic energy after passing through the rotor so that it can continue flowing downstream. If all of the kinetic energy were extracted, the air would come to a complete stop behind the turbine, preventing any further airflow through the rotor and making continuous power generation impossible.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary advantage of offshore wind farms compared with onshore wind farms?

options.text: They eliminate the need for transmission infrastructure.
They generally experience stronger and more consistent wind resources.
They require smaller turbines to achieve the same power output.
They are less expensive to install and maintain.

questions.explanation: Offshore locations typically experience higher average wind speeds and lower turbulence than land-based sites. These conditions increase energy production and improve the capacity factor of offshore wind turbines, making offshore wind farms an attractive option despite their higher installation and maintenance costs.

questions.stem: A passive solar building receives 5,000 kWh of useful solar heat through its south-facing windows during the winter. If the building experiences a total heat loss of 4,000 kWh over the same period, what is the additional heating energy required from a backup heating system?
questions.explanation: The solar heat gain (5,000 kWh) exceeds the building's heat loss (4,000 kWh). Since the available solar heat is sufficient to offset all heat losses, no additional heating is required from a backup system. The excess 1,000 kWh represents a net heat surplus.

questions.stem: For a fixed solar photovoltaic (PV) system in the Northern Hemisphere, increasing the panel tilt angle beyond the annual optimum generally helps to

options.text: increase winter energy capture when the sun is lower in the sky
increase summer energy capture when the sun is nearly overhead
eliminate reflection losses from the panel surface
maintain the same solar incidence angle throughout the year

questions.explanation: In winter, the sun follows a lower path across the sky. A steeper panel tilt improves the angle at which sunlight strikes the module, thereby increasing winter solar energy capture.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an active solar heating system from a passive solar heating system?

options.text: Collection of solar energy through south-facing glazing
Storage of heat in materials with high thermal mass
Distribution of heat by natural convection and radiation
Heat transfer assisted by pumps or fans

questions.explanation: Active solar heating systems use mechanical devices such as pumps or fans to circulate a heat-transfer fluid and distribute solar heat. Passive solar heating systems rely on building design, thermal mass, and natural heat transfer mechanisms such as conduction, convection, and radiation. MSQ (5 � 2 = 10)

questions.stem: Which of the following factors are typically considered when estimating the technical potential of solar energy in a region?
questions.explanation: Technical potential accounts for resource availability, suitable installation area, and technology performance. Electricity prices are relevant to economic potential.

questions.stem: Which of the following are potential environmental concerns associated with wind energy projects?

options.text: Bird and bat mortality due to turbine collisions
Habitat fragmentation caused by access roads and supporting infrastructure
Noise and shadow-flicker effects on nearby communities
Alteration of local landscape aesthetics and visual character

questions.explanation: Although wind energy produces electricity with minimal direct emissions, wind farms may raise environmental concerns related to wildlife impacts, habitat disturbance, noise and shadow flicker, and visual effects on the surrounding landscape.

questions.stem: Which of the following pathways can be used to produce green hydrogen directly using solar energy?
questions.explanation: Photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems use sunlight directly to drive water-splitting reactions. In contrast, photovoltaic- powered and solar-powered electrolysis first convert solar energy into electricity, which is then used to produce hydrogen.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors can influence the electrical output of a photovoltaic (PV) module?

options.text: Solar irradiance incident on the module surface
Shading of individual cells within the module
Orientation and tilt angle of the module

questions.explanation: PV output is influenced by the amount of sunlight received, module temperature, shading effects, and installation geometry.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a potential environmental challenge associated with the large-scale deployment of renewable energy technologies?

options.text: Unintended lifecycle carbon footprints from the manufacturing and disposal of renewable energy components
Ecological fragmentation and shifts in biodiversity due to large-scale renewable infrastructure
Accelerated resource depletion and environmental degradation linked to the mining of critical raw materials for green technologies
Increased reliance on geologically constrained and environmentally disruptive energy storage solutions

questions.explanation: Large-scale renewable energy technologies can pose environmental challenges, such as carbon footprints from manufacturing and disposal, ecological disruption affecting biodiversity, and resource depletion due to the mining of critical materials needed for these technologies.

questions.stem: Which of the following geothermal energy technologies involves creating engineered underground reservoirs by enhancing or artificially stimulating rock formations, thereby enabling the extraction of geothermal energy from locations that would otherwise be inaccessible?
questions.explanation: Enhanced geothermal systems create artificial underground reservoirs by injecting fluid into hot, impermeable rock formations to improve permeability and heat extraction. This allows geothermal energy to be harnessed from regions where natural geothermal reservoirs are absent or inaccessible.

questions.stem: A tidal barrage power plant has a basin area of 470 km2 and operates with a tidal range of 8 m. The tidal cycle period is 12 h. Assuming a seawater density of 1000 kg m3 and gravitational acceleration of 9.81 m s2, what is the approximate average power output of the plant?
questions.explanation: The average power (Pavg) harvested from a tidal basin is (.g.A.h2) / (2T) Given: = 1000 kg m3, g = 9.81 m s2, A = 470 � 106 m2, h = 8 m, T = 12 � 3600 s Substituting, Pavg = (1000 � 9.81 � 470 � 106 � 82) / (2 � 12 � 3600) = 3.42 � 109 W = 3.4 GW

questions.stem: Which of the following ocean energy technologies has the largest estimated global technical energy potential?
questions.explanation: OTEC exploits the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep ocean water. Because tropical oceans cover vast areas and operate continuously, OTEC has the largest estimated global technical potential, often exceeding 44,000 TWh per year, which is significantly greater than the estimated potentials of tidal, wave, or salinity-gradient energy technologies.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): Fast pyrolysis produces bio-oil by rapidly heating biomass in the absence of oxygen. Reason (R): The absence of oxygen prevents combustion and enables the thermal decomposition of biomass into liquid products.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Fast pyrolysis involves heating biomass rapidly in an oxygen-free environment. The absence of oxygen prevents the biomass from burning and instead promotes thermal decomposition, producing bio-oil as the major product along with biochar and syngas. Therefore, the reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.stem: Point absorbers and attenuators are classified as oscillating-body wave energy converters because they primarily

options.text: convert pressure waves propagating through a flexible, water-filled tube into electrical energy.
convert the oscillatory motion of floating or submerged structures induced by ocean waves into useful power.
generate electricity from bidirectional airflow produced by the oscillation of a water column.
harness the potential energy of seawater collected in an elevated reservoir by wave overtopping.

questions.explanation: Point absorbers and attenuators generate electricity by converting the oscillatory motion of floating or submerged structures induced by ocean waves into useful power. This wave-induced body motion is the defining feature of oscillating-body wave energy converters.

questions.stem: A hydroelectric power plant operates at a head of 55 m with a water flow rate of 500 m3 s�1 through the turbines. If the overall efficiency of the plant is 77%, calculate the electricity generation capacity. Assume water density = 1000 kg m�1 and g = 9.81 m s-2.
questions.explanation: Mass flow of water (mw) = 500 m3 s�1 � 1000 kg m�3 = 500,000 kg s�1 Therefore, Pelec = ehydromwg(z) = 0.77 � 500,000 � 9.81 � 55 = 2.07 � 108 W = 207 MW

questions.stem: In the anaerobic digestion of food waste, which stage involves the breakdown of complex organic polymers such as carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids into simpler soluble compounds that can be utilized by microorganisms?
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis is the first stage of anaerobic digestion, during which complex organic matter is converted into simpler soluble molecules such as sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids, making them available for subsequent microbial degradation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes third-generation biofuels from first- and second- generation biofuels?

options.text: They are produced exclusively from food crops such as corn and sugarcane.
They are derived from lignocellulosic biomass such as agricultural residues and woody biomass.
They are produced primarily from algae and other high-lipid microorganisms.
They are synthesized directly from fossil fuels blended with ethanol.

questions.explanation: Third-generation biofuels are mainly derived from algae and other microorganisms, which can achieve high biomass productivity without competing directly with food crops.

questions.stem: Wave energy is often described as an indirect form of solar energy because

options.text: Solar heating of the Earth's surface generates winds that transfer energy to ocean waves.
Solar radiation directly heats ocean water, producing surface waves.
Wave motion is primarily caused by the thermal expansion of seawater.
Ocean waves are generated by tidal forces induced by solar radiation.

questions.explanation: Most ocean waves are generated by wind. Since winds are driven by the uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun, wave energy is considered an indirect form of solar energy.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics distinguishes geothermal energy from many other renewable energy resources?

options.text: It is available only during daylight hours.
It can provide reliable, continuous baseload power.
Its output is directly governed by seasonal weather conditions.
It relies on large-scale energy storage to ensure a stable power supply.

questions.explanation: Unlike many renewable energy sources that are influenced by weather conditions, geothermal energy can provide a continuous and reliable supply of power, making it well-suited for baseload electricity generation. MSQ (5 � 2 = 10)

questions.stem: Which of the following are potential benefits of biomass pretreatment intended for biofuel production?

options.text: Increasing the surface area available for enzymatic hydrolysis.
Reducing cellulose crystallinity and improving enzyme accessibility.
Disrupting the lignin�carbohydrate matrix to expose fermentable polysaccharides.
Directly converting cellulose and hemicellulose into biofuels during the pretreatment step.

questions.explanation: The primary goals of biomass pretreatment are to increase enzyme accessibility by modifying the physical and chemical structure of lignocellulosic biomass. Pretreatment facilitates subsequent hydrolysis and fermentation but does not directly convert biomass into biofuels.

questions.stem: Which of the following environmental impacts are commonly associated with the construction and operation of large hydroelectric dams?

options.text: Alteration of natural river flow patterns.
Disruption of fish migration and aquatic ecosystems.
Submergence of terrestrial habitats due to reservoir formation.
Emission of fly ash during electricity generation.

questions.explanation: Large hydroelectric dams can modify natural river flow regimes, impede fish migration, and inundate terrestrial ecosystems through reservoir creation. Fly ash emissions are associated with coal-fired power plants and do not occur during hydroelectric power generation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about tidal energy are correct?

options.text: It is driven primarily by the gravitational interaction of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.
It is one of the most predictable renewable energy resources.
Tidal barrages utilize differences in water level across a basin.
The magnitude of tidal currents and tidal ranges is largely independent of local coastal geography.

questions.explanation: Tidal energy is governed by gravitational forces and is highly predictable. Tidal barrages exploit differences in water levels, while local coastal geometry strongly influences tidal ranges and current velocities.

questions.stem: Which of the following are common direct-use applications of geothermal energy (i.e., where geothermal heat is utilized without first being converted into electricity?

options.text: District heating of residential and commercial buildings.
Heating of greenhouses for year-round crop production.

questions.explanation: Geothermal heat can be used directly for space heating, greenhouse heating, and aquaculture. Transportation systems are generally powered by liquid fuels, electricity, or hydrogen rather than direct geothermal heat.

questions.stem: Which of the following are recognized environmental benefits associated with the production and use of biodiesel?

options.text: Complete elimination of exhaust emissions from diesel engines.
Reduced environmental persistence in the event of accidental spills.
Valorization of waste oils and animal fats as feedstocks.

questions.explanation: Biodiesel can reduce dependence on petroleum fuels, is generally more biodegradable in the event of accidental spills, and can be produced from waste oils and animal fats. However, biodiesel combustion still generates exhaust emissions and does not eliminate them completely.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities is not an example of reuse?

options.text: Refilling a beverage bottle for repeated use
Using a refillable shopping bag multiple times
Melting and reprocessing plastic bottles to manufacture new bottles
Donating used clothing for continued use by others

questions.explanation: Reuse involves using a product again with little or no modification, whereas recycling involves processing waste materials to create new products. Option (c) is an example of recycling, not reuse.

questions.stem: According to the circular economy hierarchy, which of the following sequences correctly arranges the listed "R" strategies in increasing order of circularity (from least circular to most circular)?
questions.explanation: Recycling recovers materials after a product reaches the end of its useful life and is generally less circular than strategies that retain product value. Repurposing gives a product a new function, while repairing extends its original use with minimal resource input. Rethinking involves redesigning products, services, or consumption patterns to avoid waste generation in the first place and is therefore considered the most circular strategy among the options.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): Industrial symbiosis can improve resource efficiency within an industrial cluster. Reason (R): The waste or by-products generated by one industry can be used as inputs by another industry.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Industrial symbiosis enhances resource efficiency by facilitating the exchange of materials, energy, and by-products among industries. The reason directly explains the assertion.

questions.stem: A company decides to remanufacture electric motors instead of producing new ones. A life-cycle assessment shows that manufacturing a new motor results in 5.0 tonnes of CO2 emissions, whereas remanufacturing an existing motor results in 1.5 tonnes of CO2 emissions. If the company remanufactures 65 motors, how much CO2 emissions are avoided compared with manufacturing the same number of new motors?
questions.explanation: Emission savings per motor: 5.0 � 1.5 = 3.5 tonnes CO2 For 65 motors: 65 � 3.5 = 227.5 tonnes CO2 Remanufacturing each motor avoids 3.5 tonnes of CO2 emissions compared with manufacturing a new motor. Therefore, remanufacturing 65 motors results in a total emissions savings of 227.5 tonnes of CO2.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates a "rethink" strategy in a circular economy, where a product or system is fundamentally redesigned to deliver greater value and resource efficiency?

options.text: Designing beverage containers that can be returned, cleaned, and refilled multiple times.
Recovering phosphorus from municipal wastewater for fertilizer production.
Replacing individual office printers with a centralized on-demand printing service.
Repairing industrial motors to extend their operational lifespan.

questions.explanation: A rethink strategy involves fundamentally changing how a product or service is delivered to reduce resource consumption and improve utilization. Replacing individual printers with a shared on-demand printing service rethinks the conventional ownership model. In contrast, options (a), (b), and (d) represent reuse, resource recovery, and repair, respectively.

questions.stem: Within the framework of a circular economy, what is the most significant advantage of repurposing or recycling decommissioned wind turbine blades?

options.text: It reduces the need for landfill disposal while retaining the value embedded in composite materials.
It decreases the environmental impacts associated with the extraction and processing of virgin construction materials.
It creates opportunities for secondary applications such as bridges, noise barriers, and architectural structures.
It extends the usefulness of blade materials beyond their original function, thereby slowing resource throughput in the economy.

questions.explanation: All four statements are valid benefits. However, from a circular economy perspective, the most fundamental objective is to retain the value of materials for as long as possible and reduce the flow of virgin resources through the economy. Repurposing wind turbine blades directly achieves this by extending the useful life of embedded materials.

questions.stem: Two cities consume the same quantity of energy and materials each year. City A recovers and reuses a substantial fraction of its waste streams, whereas City B primarily relies on landfill disposal. Which statement best describes the likely difference in their urban metabolisms?

options.text: City A is likely to have a lower material throughput per unit of useful service delivered.
City A is likely to exhibit higher material circulation within the system and lower dependence on virgin resource inputs.
City A is likely to accumulate waste stocks more rapidly because recovered materials remain within the city.
City A is likely to have a larger metabolic footprint because resource recovery processes require additional energy and infrastructure.

questions.explanation: By recovering and reusing a larger fraction of its waste streams, City A keeps materials in productive use for longer periods, increasing material circulation within the urban system. This reduces the need for virgin resource extraction and reflects a more circular and resource-efficient urban metabolism compared with City B, which primarily relies on landfill disposal.

questions.stem: Match the following circular business models with their most appropriate defining characteristics. Circular Business Model Key Characteristic

options.text: Circular supplies 1. Providing access to a product through leasing or subscription rather than ownership
Product as a service 2. Using renewable, recyclable, or sustainably sourced inputs
Product life extension 3. Extending product usability through repair, refurbishment, or remanufacturing
Sharing platform 4. Enabling the shared use of underutilized products or assets

questions.explanation: Circular supplies rely on renewable or recyclable inputs, while product-as-a-service models provide access to products without transferring ownership. Product life extension focuses on repair and remanufacturing, whereas sharing platforms increase the utilization of underused assets through collaborative access.

questions.stem: Two companies adopt different approaches for managing end-of-life office chairs. One company repairs damaged chairs and returns them to service, while the other recycles the chairs by processing them into raw materials for new products. According to the Butterfly Diagram of the circular economy, why is the first approach generally considered more circular?

options.text: Repair requires less labor and economic activity than recycling.
Repair preserves a greater proportion of the product's embodied value than material recycling.
Repair completely eliminates the need for future resource extraction.
Repair prevents the generation of waste throughout the product life cycle.

questions.explanation: The Butterfly Diagram prioritizes strategies that retain the highest value of products, components, and materials. By keeping the chair in use with minimal processing, repair preserves more embodied value than recycling, which breaks the product down to its constituent materials.

questions.stem: A city achieves a recycling rate of 95% for aluminum cans. Which statement best reflects a key limitation of relying solely on circular economy strategies to achieve long-term resource sustainability?

options.text: High recycling rates can substantially reduce demand for primary aluminum, but may not eliminate it because material losses occur and overall consumption can continue to grow.
Once recycling rates exceed a critical threshold, the aluminum cycle becomes effectively self-sustaining and independent of virgin resource inputs.
High recycling rates ensure that the environmental impacts associated with aluminum production are largely eliminated over time.
Increasing recycling efficiency is sufficient to decouple economic growth from resource extraction under all circumstances.

questions.explanation: Even highly efficient recycling systems experience material losses, and increasing consumption can outpace gains from resource recovery. Therefore, high recycling rates alone do not guarantee complete circularity or eliminate the need for virgin resource extraction. .

questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding water resources and water use: I. Groundwater constitutes a larger share of freshwater resources than all fresh surface water combined. II. Since groundwater forms nearly one-third of freshwater resources, it is generally more accessible than surface water. III. The amount of usable freshwater on Earth is less than 0.1% of the planet's total water resources. IV. Most freshwater surface water is stored in rivers. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: I. Correct. Groundwater constitutes about 30.1% of freshwater resources, whereas surface water accounts for only about 0.3%.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding water withdrawal and consumption: I. Water used for drinking and cooking is generally considered a return flow. II. Municipal wastewater discharge can exceed municipal water supply. III. Water used for bathing generally contributes to wastewater generation. IV. Domestic water use in urban areas is predominantly non-consumptive in nature. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: I. Incorrect. Water used for drinking and cooking is a consumptive use and is generally not returned directly to the water source.

questions.stem: Consider the following pollution sources: I. Industrial effluent discharged through a pipeline. II. Stormwater runoff from urban roads. III. Agricultural runoff carrying fertilizers and pesticides. IV. Wastewater treatment plant discharge. V. Leachate entering a river through a distinct and identifiable channel. How many of the above are point sources of pollution?
questions.explanation: Point sources are pollution sources that originate from a specific, identifiable location such as a pipe, drain, or outlet. Source I is a point source because industrial effluent is discharged through a clearly identifiable pipeline. Source II is a non-point source.

questions.stem: Assertion (A): A wastewater sample having a higher ThOD than another sample may exhibit a lower BOD. Reason (R): ThOD represents the total oxygen required for complete chemical oxidation, whereas BOD depends on the biodegradable fraction oxidized within five days. Choose the correct option:

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: ThOD represents the theoretical oxygen required for complete oxidation of a compound. BOD represents the oxygen consumed due to biological oxidation during the first five days. A sample may have a high ThOD but contain compounds that are not readily biodegradable.

The resulting river-water mixture has an ultimate biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of 15.2 mg/L and a dissolved oxygen concentration of 7.2 mg/L.
